query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The onset and progression of the phase transition in initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by a surface‐driven compositional segregation mechanism, where the low-melting Cu component migrates to the nanoparticle surface. This local enrichment lowers the melting temperature at the surface, triggering premelting that then propagates into the particle core.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with an initially homogeneous elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Heat nanoparticles under controlled conditions (specific ramp rate in an inert atmosphere, e.g., Ar) with one set left untreated and a controlled comparison set modified to inhibit surface diffusion (for example, by applying a thin chemical coating or ligand that retards Cu migration).
generation.conditions: Temperature ramp through the premelting regime into full melting (near the melting point of the alloy), in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with identical heating times and ramp rates for both sets.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a core-shell structure, where a thin Cu-enriched (and thus lower melting) liquid-like surface layer forms prior to the melting of the bulk.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, atomic mobility at the nanoparticle surface increases, enabling Cu atoms (with a lower intrinsic melting point) to segregate to the surface. This segregation lowers the local solid–liquid interfacial energy, triggering the onset of surface melting (premelting), which then acts as a pathway for the propagation of melting inward.
generation.predicted_outcome: Untreated nanoparticles will exhibit early signs of premelting via the appearance of a liquid-like, Cu-enriched surface layer (observable via in situ TEM or energy dispersive spectroscopy) and a measurable reduction in the onset temperature of melting (via DSC). In contrast, diffusion-inhibited (coated) nanoparticles will show delayed or reduced premelting behavior and a higher, closer-to-expected melting point relative to the untreated baseline.
generation.baseline: Untreated, homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles under the same thermal conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under conditions where thermal energy is sufficient to mobilize surface atoms (in the premelting regime) but before full bulk melting; deviations may occur if severe oxidation or other environmental interactions take place.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of Cu segregation and its quantitative impact on the melting temperature is uncertain, as nanoscale diffusivity and interfacial energies may vary with nanoparticle size distribution and slight compositional fluctuations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles: one set remains untreated, while the other is coated with a thin, diffusion-limiting ligand. Heat both sets under identical inert atmosphere conditions through the range spanning premelting to full melting. Use in situ TEM with EDS to monitor surface composition changes and DSC to measure the onset temperature of melting.
measurements: Surface chemical composition over temperature (EDS mapping)
Image-based detection of liquid-like surface layer (in situ TEM)
Heat flow and phase transition onset temperature (DSC)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both untreated and coated nanoparticles exhibit similar early onset of surface premelting (i.e., similar Cu surface enrichment and melting onset temperatures), then the hypothesis that Cu surface segregation is the controlling factor is falsified.
